news_communities.title: DiDomenico Welcomes Sales Tax-free Weekend
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Senator Sal DiDomenico and his colleagues in the Massachusetts Legislature set Saturday, August 8 and Sunday, August 9 as the official dates of Massachusetts’ annual sales tax holiday. During the holiday, the state’s 6.25 percent sales tax will be suspended for most retail items priced under $2,500.  

A 2018 state law, which made the sales tax holiday permanent, requires the Legislature to vote to set the dates of the holiday each year. Both branches adopted resolutions setting this year’s dates (H.5495/S.3119), sponsored by Representative Carole A. Fiola (D-Fall River) and by Senator Nick Collins (D-South Boston). 

“As prices shoot up on all kinds of products thanks to tariffs and foreign wars, this year’s temporary suspension of the sales tax will bring needed relief to consumers while supporting small businesses across the state,” said Senator Sal N. DiDomenico. “I encourage all my residents to take advantage of this weekend, and I look forward to the increased economic activity for stores throughout my district.”

A spike in consumer activity routinely boosts indirect tax revenues. According to the Department of Revenue, the 2025 sales tax holiday generated $3.65 million in indirect tax revenues due to increased economic activity.  

At a time when consumers are seeing prices on store shelves rise, driven in part by federally imposed tariffs, this year’s Massachusetts sales tax holiday will give shoppers a much-needed break. The holiday also encourages families looking to shop for back-to-school season to support local small businesses and retailers.  

Information about eligible purchases is available on the Department of Revenue website.

news_communities.title: Commissioner Rejects Proposed Rate Increase from Fallon Community Health Plan
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

Governor Maura Healey announced that the Division of Insurance has negotiated down proposed rate increases from seven health insurers, saving Massachusetts residents and businesses a projected $72 million in health care premiums for 2027.  

The Division of Insurance re-negotiated lower rates with Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts HMO Blue, INC., Harvard Pilgrim Health Care, Health New England, Mass General Brigham Health Plan, Tufts Health Public Plans, United Healthcare and WellSense Health Plan. These efforts will result in savings for the approximately 670,000 Massachusetts residents and businesses who are enrolled in these plans in the Massachusetts merged market.

Commissioner Michael Caljouw also rejected Fallon Community Health Plan’s proposed 25.7% rate increase for being excessive and inconsistent with his responsibility to Massachusetts consumers and businesses. This disapproval is now subject to an administrative appeal process should the insurance company choose one.

“Massachusetts residents and businesses are already struggling with the high cost of health care. Nobody can afford massive increases in their health insurance premiums on top of that,” said Governor Healey. “Commissioner Caljouw and his team are always looking for ways to lower people’s costs – whether that’s by capping co-pays and deductibles or removing prior authorizations. Now, he’s saving people tens of millions of dollars next year by negotiating with affordability as his focus.”

Last year, Governor Healey signed legislation that increased the Division of Insurance’s consideration of affordability during his review of the merged market rate filings. As a result, Commissioner Caljouw was able to initially save residents and businesses $54 million in 2026 by re-negotiating rate increases. Governor Healey has also taken action to cap health care co-pays and deductibles for the first time in Massachusetts history, and further lowered that cap this year to save people an estimated average of $232 per year. She also eliminated prior authorization requirements for many routine and essential health care services, reducing delays and administrative costs for patients and providers, and prohibited medical debt from appearing on consumer credit reports

news_communities.title: Healey-Driscoll Administration Expands Firefighter Survival Training with New Mobile SCBA Maze
news_communities.author: Independent Staff
news_communities.summary:
Special to the Independent

The Massachusetts Department of Fire Services (DFS) announced the expansion of firefighter survival training at the Massachusetts Firefighting Academy (MFA) with the addition of a new mobile self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) training maze. The new training system will increase access to realistic, hands-on instruction for recruit and veteran municipal firefighters across the Commonwealth.

“One of DFS’s most important responsibilities is ensuring firefighters across Massachusetts have access to the highest-quality training possible,” said Public Safety and Security Secretary Gina Kwon. “That means continually investing in modern equipment and training environments that reflect the dangerous and unpredictable conditions firefighters face in the field. Better training builds more confident, better prepared firefighters, and better prepared firefighters help make communities across Massachusetts safer.”

The new mobile training maze expands the MFA’s ability to deliver firefighter survival training both on campus and directly to local fire departments. Combined with the Academy’s existing mobile training resources, it will increase access to realistic, hands-on SCBA training for recruits and experienced firefighters alike. The unit also replaces the Academy’s original Stow-based SCBA maze, ensuring this critical training remains available for years to come.

This year, DFS marks 30 years of training Massachusetts firefighters through the MFA. Since 1996, the Academy has prepared thousands of firefighters for the challenges of the job while continually evolving its training programs to reflect new technologies, emerging hazards, and best practices. The addition of the new mobile SCBA training maze builds on that legacy by giving more firefighters the opportunity to train in realistic, high-pressure environments that build the skills and confidence they need to respond safely and effectively when lives are on the line.

“The SCBA Training Maze is one of our most frequently requested training tools,” said State Fire Marshal Jon M. Davine. “This new mobile unit allows us to deliver critical survival training to more firefighters in more communities while strengthening the MFA’s ability to prepare recruits and veteran firefighters for the dangerous and unpredictable conditions they face. Providing firefighters with realistic training is one of the best investments we can make in their safety and the safety of the communities they serve.”

Inside the maze, firefighters navigate dark, confined, and unfamiliar environments while wearing full turnout gear and SCBA. The training is designed to build confidence under stress, improve air management, and reinforce the skills firefighters rely on during searches, rescues, and self-extrication.

Last year, the MFA’s Springfield-based mobile SCBA maze supported training for more than 500 municipal firefighters. The addition of a second roadworthy mobile unit will expand training opportunities for fire departments across Massachusetts while continuing to support recruit training at the Stow campus.

The new mobile maze is one of several investments that have strengthened training at the MFA in recent years, alongside a forcible entry trailer, flashover training prop, search and rescue buildings on the Bridgewater and Springfield campuses, a hazardous materials leak prop, and a Mobile Extraction Unit used to decontaminate firefighting gear.

DFS invested approximately $500,000 in the new training system, supported in large part by a $435,000 FEMA Assistance to Firefighters Grant. The investment reflects DFS’s continued commitment to providing firefighters across Massachusetts with access to realistic, state-of-the-art training.

news_communities.title: A dozen wins lift Seasiders to playoffs
news_communities.author: Joey BarrettJoey BarrettJoey Barrett
news_communities.summary:
MARBLEHEAD — After last summer’s eight-win season and the team typically finishing with less than 10 wins, the Marblehead Seasiders have turned a big page.

The Seasiders, of the 10-team North Shore Baseball League, stand at 12-11-1. Their 25 points has them in fifth place and holding a playoff spot.

“We’re in the playoffs, which won’t begin until Sunday or Monday,” said founder Joe McKane. “We’ll probably be a bottom-four team, which means we’re going to have to play some away games.”

The Red and White racked up a pair of wins against Swampscott last weekend, followed by Monday night’s victory against North Reading. Wilbur Rosario and newly-acquired David Stepan each smashed home runs.

When asked about this summer’s success and turnaround, McKane was quick to respond.

“We won a lot of close games,” he said. “Mike Mitchell and Brennan Frost made a real effort in the offseason to get some more guys, and it worked. … Frost was our best pitcher and won a couple of games, too.”

According to the league’s online statistics, Marblehead’s offensive contributors have been Trey Blackmer (10 H, 10 R, 8 RBI, 9 BB), Rosario (15 H, 12 R), Stepan (11 H, 7 R, 7 RBI, 5 BB), Enrique Quinonez (6 H, 9 R, 7 RBI, 6 BB), Spencer Merrick (9 H, 3 R, 7 RBI, 5 BB), Ben Shea (7 H, 5 R, 3 RBI, 2 BB), Mitchell (7 H, 7 R, 6 RBI, 10 BB), Frost (13 H, 6 R, 8 RBI, 5 BB), Connor McNamara (6 H, 4 R, 4 RBI, 2 BB), and Gabe Fales (9 H, 6 R, 3 RBI, 6 BB).

“We’ve made the playoffs a couple of times in the last 10 years and we’d like to get to the next round. We want to win the first round and along with 12 wins, that’d be good,” McKane said. “We’re looking forward to the offseason with Seaside (Park) getting done, the infield especially, so when it rains, we don’t have to wait three days to play. That’ll be exciting.”

news_communities.title: Gannon crowns its champions after close finishes
news_communities.author: Joey BarrettJoey BarrettJoey Barrett
news_communities.summary:
LYNN — The men’s innerclub at Gannon Municipal Golf Course has crowned its champions after back-to-back weekends of match play, as well as an additional 36 holes.

In a close finish, Jay Fiste won the 36th hole to beat Mike Bono, 1-up and win the club championship.

Fiste, also the varsity golf coach at St. Mary’s, captured his second club title in three years.

“Mike Bono and I are very good friends. We knew, from the start, it was going to be a tight final 36-hole match and it came right down to hole 36. The match could easily have gone either way,” Fiste said. “Match play is much less stressful at the beginning of a round than it is down the stretch. Trying to close out a match against an excellent player is not easy and mistakes escalate. I was up 3 holes at two different times, but Mike came back each time. I finally won on the 36th hole.”

Mike Marks defeated Pat McHale, 3-and-2, for the net club title, while Mike Sullivan took down Paul Gorman in the senior club championship, 4-and-2.

news_communities.title: Marblehead Board of Health debates kratom sales
news_communities.author: Sophia HarrisSophia HarrisSophia Harris
news_communities.summary:
MARBLEHEAD — The Marblehead Board of Health is considering a regulation that would prohibit the sale, manufacture and distribution of kratom products, citing concerns about public health and the growing availability of products that are largely unregulated.

The draft regulation, which the board discussed at Tuesday night’s meeting, would ban both natural leaf kratom and synthetically derived kratom products, along with synthetic cannabinoids such as delta-8 and delta-10 THC and other “unregulated novel intoxicating products.”

According to the proposal, the regulation is intended to reduce access to products the board says may present health risks because they are often sold without consistent labeling, dosage information, or ingredient transparency.

The proposal defines natural leaf kratom as leaves from the Mitragyna speciosa plant that have not been chemically altered or mixed with other ingredients. It separately defines synthetically derived kratom as products whose alkaloids have been artificially increased through chemical synthesis or concentrated beyond naturally occurring levels.

During the meeting, board members discussed whether kratom products are currently sold in Marblehead.

When asked whether the products could be found at local retailers, Public Health Director Andrew Petty said tobacco inspectors regularly visit stores but are not specifically inspecting for kratom because it is currently legal.

“They are looking for this product, but it’s not the products that they’re going after,” Petty said.

When asked whether kratom could legally be sold in town under current regulations, Petty said he would need to review existing state law.

“I’d have to take a look exactly what the law is because the Division of Agriculture does have some regulations on certain things,” he said.

Petty added that while there are places where the products could legally be sold, he did not believe they are currently available in Marblehead, though he did not say that definitively.

Board member Tom McMahon cautioned that kratom can be used to help manage opioid dependency and chronic pain management.

He added that although he did not have all of the information, he cautioned board members that taking away the substance may push people to consume more dangerous drugs.

Petty said that surrounding communities have already banned the substance, including Beverly, Salem, Saugus, and Peabody.

If adopted, violations of the regulation would carry escalating penalties. A first violation would result in a $1,000 fine. A second violation within 36 months would carry another $1,000 fine and a seven-business-day suspension of any Board of Health-issued permit. A third violation would result in another $1,000 fine and a 30-business-day permit suspension. After a fourth violation within 36 months, the board could permanently revoke a permit following a public hearing.

The draft also allows the Board of Health to suspend or revoke permits immediately following a hearing if it determines a violation has occurred.

The proposal exempts cannabis products sold through state-licensed medical and adult-use dispensaries regulated by the Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission.

Kratom is a plant native to Southeast Asia whose leaves have traditionally been used for stimulant and pain-relieving effects. In recent years, concentrated products containing 7-hydroxymitragynine, commonly known as 7-OH, have become increasingly available in the United States. Health officials have raised concerns that these highly concentrated products can produce opioid-like effects and may pose greater risks than traditional kratom leaf products.

As part of the discussion, board members received informational material comparing concentrated synthetic 7-OH products with natural kratom leaf. The handout described concentrated 7-OH products as laboratory-made, highly concentrated substances often sold as tablets, gummies, or other novelty products, while distinguishing them from traditional natural leaf kratom sold in powder, tea, or capsule form.

Despite those distinctions, the draft regulation would prohibit both natural leaf kratom and synthetically derived kratom products.

The Board of Health is expected to continue discussing the proposal before taking action on whether to adopt the regulation.

The post Marblehead Board of Health debates kratom sales appeared first on Itemlive.

news_communities.title: Swampscott approves Littles Point project
news_communities.author: Erin HickeyErin HickeyErin Hickey
news_communities.summary:
SWAMPSCOTT — The Conservation Commission approved plans for shoreline restoration and outdoor construction work at 45 Littles Point Road, clearing the way for a project that will remove deteriorating concrete, relocate beach access, and replace invasive vegetation with native plantings at one of Swampscott’s most valuable waterfront homes. 

The commission unanimously issued an order of conditions for the work after adding a few environmental safeguards aimed at protecting the property’s coastal resource areas during and after construction. 

Landscape designer Jonathan Keep attended the meeting to represent the homeowners, and said the proposal consisted of four primary elements: removing a deteriorating concrete slab from the rocky shoreline, relocating an existing fieldstone staircase, restoring the coastal bank with primarily native vegetation, and creating a small dry-laid fieldstone sitting area above the bank. 

Keep said the concrete slab, which dates to before 1995, has been broken apart by years of coastal storms and will be removed rather than being replaced. 

“It shows up in a 1995 survey when the current house was built,” Keep said. “We’re proposing to remove an existing dry-laid fieldstone access stair to the rocky beach and create a ramp that would allow a bobcat access to the rocky beach and to remove broken-up pieces of the slab, which would be taken to a dumpster at the front of the house and taken off to a recycling facility.” 

The proposal would also relocate an existing stone staircase approximately 60 feet east along the coastal bank. Keep said the new location was selected to improve safety by moving beach access away from a section of shoreline with a steep drop. 

“The primary reason for moving it is that there is an inlet there with a concrete seawall and there’s like a 15-foot drop,” Keep said. “So we’re just trying to move any visitors to the rocky beach kind of away from that dangerous condition.” 

Another significant component of the project involves removing invasive vegetation from the coastal bank and replacing it with native trees, shrubs, grasses, and perennials intended to stabilize the slope and better withstand coastal conditions. 

“The goal is to create a robust native plant community on that bank that can withstand salt spray and the wind and also absorb any water runoff,” Keep said, adding that based on feedback from a site visit with commission members, the landscaping would be monitored for two years with dead plants and invasive grow-backs replaced and removed as needed. 

Because the work falls within a coastal bank and land subject to coastal storm flow, it required review under the Massachusetts Wetlands Protection Act. Conservation Commission Chair Toni Bandrowicz said the commission’s focus was ensuring the project protects the shoreline’s environmental function. 

“The important thing is that whatever work or project being done is not going to damage the integrity of the coastal bank,” Bandrowicz said. “It’s basically on a bank. It’s not going to be as concerning as if it wasn’t on a vertical bank… but there are standard conditions that will be put into any order of conditions we issued.”

Commissioners asked Keep questions regarding demolition methods, equipment storage, dust control, and long-term maintenance before approving the project. The approved order of conditions includes special requirements that construction crews wet concrete and stone during demolition to reduce dust, remove equipment from the shoreline at the end of each workday, avoid stockpiling materials within the resource area, and prioritize a majority of native species in the new plantings. 

Keep told commissioners the owners hope to begin construction in September once the permit is issued.

news_communities.title: Body found in Salem Harbor awaiting identity
news_communities.author: Sophia HarrisSophia HarrisSophia Harris
news_communities.summary:
SALEM — Police were notified Tuesday morning of a body floating in the water in the vicinity of Central Wharf.

On Tuesday, July 28, at approximately 9:40 a.m., Salem Police were notified of a body floating in the water in the vicinity of Central Wharf. 

The Salem Police said in a statement, “We are currently awaiting both the identification of the victim and a determination of the cause of death.”

The statement read, “In these situations, we avoid jumping to conclusions, but preserve whatever evidence we have in the event the case turns criminal in nature.”

Salem Police, State Police, and the office of the Essex County District Attorney have joined the investigation, which is a standard procedure in such cases. 

“We will update the public with details as they become available, and we apologize for the paucity of information,” the Salem Police Stated.

The body has been recovered, and the investigation is ongoing.

news_communities.title: Newport Folk Festival lives up to its legendary reputation
news_communities.author: Bill BrothertonBill BrothertonBill Brotherton
news_communities.summary:
NEWPORT, R.I. — Back in 1959, Lynn-born jazz impresario George Wein wanted to present Odetta and other folk singers in concert. But would the singers of spirituals, traditional, and political songs fit in at his renowned Newport Jazz Festival?

Probably.

But Wein noticed that folk music was gaining favor with America’s young adults and decided that Odetta and folkies like Pete Seeger and The Weavers deserved their own shindig. It was a hit.

Wein passed away in 2021, but the Newport Folk Festival is more popular than ever. Tickets sell out in minutes well before a single act has been announced.

The 67th annual NFF took place at Fort Adams State Park last Friday-Sunday. Performances take place on five stages daily — many overlap, meaning attendees are forever leaving in the middle of one performance and rushing to catch a bit of another. On Sunday, three of my must-see acts — Brandi Carlile, Tom Morello, and Kathleen Edwards — were on different stages at the same time.

Every year, rumors run wild that one superstar or another will perform unannounced. After all, who could have imagined that Dolly Parton, Paul Simon, and Joni Mitchell would magically appear on stage without warning.

This year, it was rumored that Taylor Swift would show up during Hayley Williams & Friends set on Friday. After all, they are BFFs and Williams attended the Taylor/Travis wedding.

Equally strong were speculations that Bruce Springsteen would sit in during Rage Against the Machine lead guitarist/political activist/rabble-rouser Morello’s Sunday set.

Neither happened, but there was no shortage of standout performances over the weekend. Yes, there was a special guest — Dave Matthews, who performed and danced with Joan Baez — during Sunday’s fest-closing set, hosted by Nathaniel Rateliff.

Every year I am most blown away by performers/bands that have escaped my radar. One — CMAT (the stage name of Ireland’s Ciara Mary-Alice Thompson) — on Sunday delivered the weekend’s best set, a high-energy, tightly choreographed hour that blended pop, indie, and alternative sounds and humor. “People tell me I remind them of an old Grecian god,” said the upfront frontwoman by way of introduction. One of her male guitarists wore women’s clothes: “This is Skirt Cobain,” she said. Delightful!

Evan Honer, backed by a rocking band, was a bundle of energy, racing around the stage and ending his set with a backflip. He is a great songwriter. “Enough happy songs,” he announced mid-set and delivered a solo-acoustic version of his “Mr. Meyers,” a heartbreaker about an older man grieving his late wife. Everyone around me was sobbing. I am tearing up just typing this. Check this guy out.

Women grabbed the spotlight on Friday, with many performers joining each other’s sets.

On the large Fort Stage, Lucy Dacus brought out some big names: Madi Diaz, Hayley Williams, Killers frontman Brandon Flowers, a duet of Jim Croce’s “Time in a Bottle.” Dacus was an amiable host and performer. Australian singer/songwriter/guitarist Courtney Barnett followed with a hard rock set that was hotter than the 90+ degree temperatures, and Courtney Marie Andrews won many new fans with her Americana/folk songs. LA-based folk/pop women-led trio Trousdale featured great harmonies, as did Boston trio Tiny Habits with its glorious cover of “Alone,” a hit for Heart.

Lily Fitts, a Topsfield native and Masconomet Regional High/UMass graduate now living in South Boston, wowed with well-written country-flavored tunes. “Lose You Now” and “I Don’t Owe You (Expletive)” have hit potential. Her parents Bill and Laurie were in the audience. They said her cover of Noah Kahan’s “Stick Season” on TikTok drew praise from Noah and impressed by her raw vocal style, Zach Bryan invited her to perform “Oklahoma City” in Los Angeles with him.

Other Newport highlights:

The Olllam (cq), a tight, expressive six-piece instrumental band whose members hail from Scotland, Ireland, and America wowed with jazzy grooves.

Amble, an Irish folk band, were also terrific, playing before a huge crowd. They played a great cover of John Prine’s “Angel From Montgomery” and their uptempo tunes would have had everyone dancing if there was room to move.

Cat Power (Chan Marshall) performed her groundbreaking 1996 album “The Greatest” from start to finish’ Fans were in heaven.

Gillian Welch and smiling hubby David Rawlings had a fine time performing Grateful Dead acoustic classics for an hour. Oh no… That earworm “Uncle John’s Band” is now stuck in my head. Darn!

Brittany Davis, who is blind, performed topical piano tunes that brought to mind Nina Simone.

The Grammy-winning Punch Brothers led by Chris Thile (mandolin), Noam Pikelny (banjo), and Chris Eldridge (guitar) amazed with their blend of bluegrass, classical, and folk. They were also hilarious. To wit: “We enjoy playing sea shanties,” said Thile. “We would now like to play a Sia Shanty” and he launched into the Australian singer-songwriter’s biggest hit: “I’m going to swing from the Chandelier.” They also performed the theme song from the movie “Jaws.”

The Lumineers gave a surprise show midday on Friday at the Bike Stage, where solar panels and festivalgoers riding bikes provide the electricity. It was a warmup for their headlining Saturday set and included a few hits and a superb cover of Bob Dylan’s “Subterranean Homesick Blues.” Newport Folk Executive Director Jay Sweet, an Essex resident, said he was impressed that attendees were so into the music that he saw only three people had their phones out to record a major band playing on such a tiny stage.

Canada’s Edwards, backed by a first-rate band, made her Newport debut 23 years after her debut album and was clearly having the time of her life, as was the large crowd that cheered her on with one ovation after another.

The overtly political Morello drew an enormous crowd that was more than ready to join in on his brutally powerful, hard-rocking Trump-bashing/pro-union/anti-fascist tunes. Woody Guthrie’s “This Land is Your Land” became a loud singalong. Even though Springsteen was a no-show, the former Rage Against the Machine lead guitarist’s cover of the boss’s “Ghost of Tom Joad” was a ferocious hard-rocking affair.

Ms. Lauryn Hill’s appearance was probably the most anticipated set of the entire festival, and it didn’t go smoothly. Her hour-long show was set to begin at 5:55 pm. The crowd clapped in anticipation and seats had been removed to give the large crowd room to dance. An emcee started playing Bob Marley’s “One Love” at about 6 p.m. Before long he was killing time, leading the audience in ridiculous time wasters/“Put your hands in the air” nonsense. It would be 31 minutes after her start time before Hill sang her first note. The crowd had started to thin out, heading to the main stage area to settle in for Hayley Williams & Friends. After three songs, none of which were the big hits, I left. I had another artist to write about, after all. Hill did sing a few of her Fugee and hit songs, I was told. When she was done she mingled with fans out near the merch stand, posing for selfies and signing autographs.

Williams’ friends included Jack Antonoff of Bleachers, Jenny Lewis of Rilo Kiley, Joy Oladokun, Remi Wolf, and many others. It was a blast.

news_communities.title: Peabody’s Family Fest returns to Emerson Park
news_communities.author: Anna BaughmanAnna BaughmanAnna Baughman
news_communities.summary:
PEABODY — Emerson Park will once again become a community gathering space for games, picnics, and family fun when the Peabody Education Foundation hosts its annual Family Fest on Saturday, Aug. 8 from 1-4 p.m. In the event of rain, Family Fest will be rescheduled to Sunday, Aug. 9 from 1-4 p.m.

For $10 per person and $20 maximum per family or group, attendees can enjoy afternoon activities including an inflatable obstacle course, face painting, music from a live DJ, and yard games out on the sprawling lawn. Food and drinks will be available for purchase, while adults can kick back and relax with wine and beer.

So far, the Peabody Education Foundation has received $7,800 in sponsorships from local businesses, families, and organizations. It is still seeking sponsors, and there are several opportunities to contribute: $1,000 supports one of Family Fest’s main attractions, $500 makes donors a community champion, $250 can support the snack stand or give a teacher a shout-out on social media, and $100 makes donors a family fun supporter. For more information, visit the PEF website, peabodyedfoundation.org.

Since 1985, the foundation has provided Peabody students with educational opportunities and resources that are beyond the budget of the school department.

PEF President and Chair Dave Gravel spearheaded Family Fest last year with the intent of raising funds for the organization’s grants program, which enhances student education through classroom projects, field trips, and much more. For example, Vice Chair Mary Bellavance said that PEF sponsors trips to museums and brings in guest speakers.

PEF has recently introduced a mental health program meant to address effects on children’s wellness after COVID. It also awards scholarships to high school seniors pursuing careers in education.

Last year, the foundation raised $130,000 just in grants for the Peabody education system. The board is hoping to invest $160,000 this year overall. The foundation’s team has no overhead, meaning that every penny raised goes into the many programs it offers.

When looking at the PEF’s impact over the years, it’s clear that the foundation has grown immeasurably.

“For a long time, people didn’t really know what PEF was, or understood the benefits of PEF,” Bellavance explained. “But over the last 10 years, we’ve been able to really get out and talk to the teachers more, talk to the schools.”

Community participation in events like Family Fest has been the backbone of the Peabody Education Foundation as they continue to grow and positively impact students’ lives.

news_communities.title: Peabody cadets win Ethics Bowl
news_communities.author: Amanda LureyAmanda LureyAmanda Lurey
news_communities.summary:
PEABODY — Two Peabody Veterans Memorial High School Air Force JROTC cadets returned home from a leadership program in Oklahoma with more than memories. Their team won first place in the Ethics Bowl competition, earning each member a $2,000 college scholarship.

Deputy Commander Meghan Burke and Operations Commander Elizabeth Hagerty, both incoming seniors, attended the Four Star Leadership program, hosted by Gen. Tommy Franks at the University of Central Oklahoma from July 18-23. The pair were among 75 students selected from more than 600 applicants worldwide to participate in the program.

Burke and Hagerty said the experience challenged them academically, strengthened their leadership abilities, and introduced them to lifelong friendships with students from across the country.

“I literally texted my mom the first night after the first speaker, and I was like, ‘My life is forever changed,’” Burke said. “It taught so much [about] how big problems aren’t that big, and they told us so many things about how you can be a leader.”

The program centers on what organizers call the “4 C’s” of leadership: character, common vision, communication, and caring. Hagerty said those principles were a major reason she decided to apply, after being encouraged by her AFJROTC instructors.

“After further research, I quickly realized that my personal values when it came to leadership aligned almost perfectly with the 4 C’s this program stands by,” Hagerty said.

Throughout the week, students attended presentations from military leaders, elected officials, and other accomplished speakers, while also participating in leadership exercises, writing persuasive speeches, and preparing for the Ethics Bowl.

Burke said one of the program’s biggest lessons was learning how to work through disagreements respectfully.

“You’re not supposed to make it into a debate at all,” Burke said of the Ethics Bowl. “You’re supposed to be finding a way for me to say my point, the other team to say their point, and then we agree on something.”

Weeks before arriving in Oklahoma, participants were assigned to six-person teams and given eight ethical scenarios to research. During the competition, teams analyzed two topics per match, attempting to reach common ground rather than defeat their opponents.

Burke and Hagerty’s team included three students from Oklahoma and one from Wyoming. After winning its preliminary matches, the team advanced to the finals and were ultimately crowned champions during the Annual Four Star Leadership Awards Banquet.

“We were shocked,” Hagerty said. “We knew we put in the work and had competitive arguments to make, but we didn’t know where other teams stood. … I’m more so happy that my team worked together, and it paid off.”

For Burke, the scholarship came as an unexpected bonus.

“I was just so proud of myself,” she said. “It really helped me realize that I am a leader, and I can do things in this world. It was just so amazing and so eye-opening. I looked right at my friend Elizabeth, and I was like, ‘We just did that.’”

Beyond the competition, both cadets said the program left a lasting impression through its demanding schedule, field trips to the Oklahoma National Memorial & Museum, the Oklahoma State Capitol, and the General Tommy Franks Leadership Institute and Museum, as well as the relationships they built with fellow participants and counselors.

“This program has changed who I was, developed who I am, and influenced who I am becoming,” Hagerty said. “I plan to apply to be a counselor next year to inspire upcoming leaders like I was.”

Both students also plan to continue pursuing military careers after graduating from PVMHS.

Burke has begun applying to the U.S. Air Force Academy, saying she hopes to continue developing as a leader through military service.

“I want to be able to lead people,” Burke said. “I want to be able to show that I had to earn my leadership, and I think the military really proves that… you wouldn’t have your position, you wouldn’t have your title, without the work.”

Hagerty plans to attend college, join Air Force ROTC, commission into the U.S. Air Force, and major in kinesiology or exercise science with the goal of becoming an Air Force physical therapist.

She also offered advice to younger students considering similar opportunities.

“Take that chance,” Hagerty said. “My favorite quote ever is: ‘If your dreams don’t scare you, they aren’t big enough.’ This quote couldn’t be any more true. Even when things scared me, I knew that I would regret it if I let my fears get the best of me.”

news_communities.title: Nahant plans for park improvements
news_communities.author: Erin HickeyErin HickeyErin Hickey
news_communities.summary:
NAHANT — Ecological restoration at Lodge Park is underway, accessibility improvements at Bailey’s Hill remain a priority, and Nahant is already beginning to look ahead to updating its Open Space and Recreation Plan years before the current one expires.

The Nahant Open Space and Recreation Plan Committee spent much of its Monday meeting reviewing progress on several ongoing conservation projects while beginning early discussions about updating the town’s Open Space and Recreation Plan, which expires in the spring of 2029.

One of the committee’s largest current initiatives is ecological restoration at Henry Cabot Lodge Park, where contractors recently began work funded through a Community Preservation Committee grant. Crews have started removing invasive woody vegetation, marking future pollinator gardens, and installing temporary signs to explain the work to visitors.

Committee Chair Trish Aldridge said five native pollinator gardens have already been staked out in locations where visitors will be able to easily see them once they’re planted.

“They also marked the five pollinator patches,” Aldridge said. “So we’re going to be planting plugs and seeds for the native pollinators. They picked visible locations so that when you were up in the meadow area walking around, you’d be able to see these patches.”

Planting is expected to take place later this year when cooler temperatures provide better growing conditions. Additional work targeting invasive Japanese knotweed is also planned.

The committee also discussed improvements planned for Bailey’s Hill, including a long-term goal of adding a wheelchair-accessible ramp to the gazebo. Although the current state-funded gazebo reconstruction project does not include funding for that ramp, members said they hope to pursue Community Preservation Committee funding during a future grant cycle.

Improving community access to Nahant’s open spaces, committee members said, remains an important goal.

“We’ve talked about wanting to do some more with accessibility and improving accessibility to open space in town,” Aldridge said. “Maybe this will be a small step in the right direction, something that’s doable.”

Committee members are also working with landscapers to incorporate native, rabbit-resistant pollinator plants around the rebuilt gazebo and are coordinating with local volunteers on future landscaping plans.

Another project moving forward is an interpretive panel highlighting Bailey’s Hill’s military history. Committee members are working with the Nahant Historical Society to obtain historic photographs and other materials for the display, which they hope will be installed near one of the former military bunkers overlooking the shoreline.

Committee member Paula Devereaux said the panel will help preserve a piece of Nahant’s history that could otherwise be forgotten.

“The military history… I think that as people get older and as the generations evolve, that there are going to be people who have no idea what that was for,” Devereaux said. 

Although Nahant’s current Open Space and Recreation Plan remains in effect until 2029, committee members said they want to begin planning early so the update process can move smoothly. The committee has contacted the Metropolitan Area Planning Council to better understand the timeline for updating the document and when the town should begin seeking technical assistance and funding.

“We’re not starting from scratch or anything,” Aldridge said. “We have a very good plan. It just will need to be updated as required.”

news_communities.title: Bar accused of overserving wrong-way driver before deadly crash has hearing
news_communities.author: Robert Goulston, Munashe Kwangwari and Kaitlin McKinley Becker
news_communities.summary:
The bar that served the man whom police say drunkenly drove down the wrong side of Route 1 and killed a Massachusetts state trooper this year is fighting to keep its liquor license.

Operators of Tribu Mexican Kitchen and Bar appeared in front of state alcohol license regulators in Chelsea Tuesday. Hernan Marrero left the restaurant on May 6 two times over the legal driving limit and crashed into Trooper Kevin Trainor’s cruiser, killing them both, prosecutors have said. They didn’t bring charges against Tribu.

Tribu is only allowed to serve alcohol during certain hours and not allowed to let people drink for free. State liquor license regulators testified that the restaurant violated the conditions of their liquor license when they served Marrero nine drinks, seven of them after hours, and didn’t charge him for those drinks.

“A licensee who sells alcohol is quote unquote bound at his own peril to keep within condition of the license,” Henry DiGiacomo, associate general counsel for the Massachusetts Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission.

Tracy Firicano, one of the attorneys representing Tribu, said in her closing statement that the owners have already taken steps to correct their actions.

“They are hard workers. They learn from their experiences. They are responsible owners,” said Firicano. “They seek guidance that will assist them in assimilating any problems they have. They are very willing to take any or all measures to protect their customers.”

Trainor’s mother attended the hearing and later shared a statement that read, in part, “The privilege of holding a liquor license comes with the responsibility to protect the public by refusing to serve visibly intoxicated patrons.”

The commission will make a decision at a later date. Their options are to suspend, revoke or modify the liquor license or take no action at all.

news_communities.title: East Boston’s Elijah Garcia continues to make his mark on the national boxing stage
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
Elijah Garcia delivered an impressive performance at his latest tournament, competing with determination, skill and sportsmanship against some of the best young boxers in the country.

In the opening round, Elijah earned a hard-fought victory over the No. 6-ranked boxer in the nation. The win provided a strong start to the tournament and demonstrated his ability to compete at the highest level.

In the second round, Elijah faced the No. 3-ranked boxer in the country in an extremely competitive bout. After a closely contested match, Elijah fell just short in a split decision.

Although the tournament did not end with the result he had hoped for, Elijah gained valuable experience against elite national competition. His performances have helped establish him as one of the top boxers in his weight class while continuing his development both as an athlete and a young man.

Elijah has already returned to the gym and is training for two major national tournaments later this year.

The USA Boxing National Open will take place in Cleveland, Ohio, from September 26 through October 3. He will then prepare for the USA Boxing National Championships in Lafayette, Louisiana, scheduled for December 5–13.

Each tournament will provide another opportunity for Elijah to test himself against the nation’s best young boxers and continue working toward his goals in the sport.

news_communities.title: City moves ahead with 9 Chelsea Street project slated for 120 units
news_communities.author: admin
news_communities.summary:
BPDA approves project that completed two public meetings earlier in the process; site of the former Rapino Funeral Home. Development long in the waiting.

The Boston Planning & Development Agency has approved a six-story, 120-unit mixed-use development at 9 Chelsea Street, a long-vacant property at the edge of Maverick Square in East Boston.

The BPDA Board approved the project on July 16, allowing the development to advance through the remaining design, permitting and compliance stages of the city’s Article 80 review process. The approximately 84,267-square-foot building will include rental housing, affordable units, ground-floor retail space and extensive improvements to the surrounding sidewalks and public realm.

March meeting highlighted community concerns

Residents and nearby stakeholders raised several concerns about the proposed development, particularly its scale and impact on the character of Maverick Square. Some residents argued that the six-story building remains too tall and imposing compared with surrounding structures and could significantly change the character of the square and adjoining neighborhood. Although the project has undergone revisions, critics continued to question whether its overall size and massing are appropriate for the site.

Parking and traffic were also major concerns. Residents pointed to an existing shortage of neighborhood parking and congestion that can become particularly difficult during snow emergencies and periods of construction. The impact of parking associated with the East Boston Neighborhood Health Center (now NeighborHealth) was also cited. Some residents questioned the project’s reliance on transit access as a reason for providing no off-street parking, arguing that even if only a portion of the building’s tenants own vehicles, the addition could place further pressure on neighborhood streets. Because residents of the development would be eligible for neighborhood parking permits, critics expressed skepticism that proximity to Maverick Station would necessarily translate into a largely car-free tenant population.

The proposed mix of apartments generated additional discussion, particularly the large number of studios and other smaller units. Residents argued that such a mix could appeal primarily to young professionals or students rather than families and questioned whether the development does enough to provide family-sized housing in a neighborhood already facing concerns about displacement. Some also raised the possibility that studio apartments could eventually be used for short-term rentals such as Airbnb. The development team responded that short-term rentals are subject to separate city regulations, zoning and registration requirements and said operating the building as short-term accommodations is not part of its business model.

The amount and type of ground-floor retail also drew criticism. Several residents said a prominent site of approximately 18,802 square feet at Maverick Square should accommodate more substantial commercial space, potentially including a grocery store or supermarket, rather than primarily smaller businesses such as cafés, salons or similar establishments.

The development team said it had tested demand with major retail brokers and contacted approximately 37 prospective tenants, including national retailers, but found little interest in a large-format location at the site. Based on that outreach, the developer concluded that smaller storefronts designed for walkable, neighborhood-serving businesses represented a more financially viable and leasable approach.

The project, proposed by 9 Chelsea Street LLC, affiliated with DND Homes, will be constructed on approximately 18,975 square feet of vacant land at Chelsea and Maverick streets.

120 Apartments Planned Near Maverick Square

Plans call for 120 rental apartments consisting of 76 studios, 25 one-bedroom units and 19 two-bedroom units.

The building will also contain approximately 5,492 square feet of ground-floor retail space divided between two commercial units. Plans include approximately 802 square feet of ground-floor amenity space, a 3,568-square-foot common roof deck and 2,254 square feet of at-grade open space.

The development is located approximately 500 feet from Maverick Station on the MBTA Blue Line and is also served by nearby bus routes and seasonal East Boston ferry service.

22 Affordable and Voucher Units

Twenty-two of the building’s apartments will be income-restricted or reserved for households using mobile housing vouchers.

Eighteen units will be income-restricted at an average of 60 percent of Area Median Income. Of those, five will be available to households earning no more than 50 percent of AMI, eight at no more than 60 percent of AMI and five at no more than 70 percent of AMI.

Another four units will be made available to households using mobile housing vouchers.

The affordable and voucher units must be distributed throughout the development and comparable in design and quality to the market-rate apartments. Affordability restrictions may remain in effect for as long as 50 years.

The project also completed the city’s Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing review. Commitments include placing all Inclusionary Zoning units on site, providing more accessible units than required, increasing the proportion of larger income-restricted units and adopting inclusive tenant-screening and marketing practices.

No Automobile Parking Planned

Despite a project metrics table listing a maximum parking allowance, the proposal itself includes no automobile parking. Instead, the project emphasizes its proximity to public transportation and bicycle facilities.

Approximately 150 bicycle spaces are planned, including long-term storage for residents and short-term bicycle parking around the building.

The developer will also contribute $49,000 toward Boston’s bikeshare program and provide space nearby for a 15-dock bikeshare station.

Sidewalk and Maverick Square Improvements

The project includes reconstruction and widening of sidewalks along Chelsea, Maverick and Bremen streets.

Improvements will include accessible pedestrian zones, permeable furnishing areas, new street trees, bicycle racks, upgraded curb ramps and improved street lighting where necessary.

Curbside regulations along Maverick Street are also expected to be modified during daytime hours to provide space for short-term pickups, rideshare vehicles and deliveries.

The developer has agreed to contribute $100,307 toward public-realm and transportation improvements identified through the Maverick Square Transportation Action Plan.

Additional community contributions include $17,000 to East Boston Main Streets to support local small businesses and $17,000 to Tree Eastie to help expand the neighborhood’s tree canopy.

Project Designed Around Transit and PLAN: East Boston

The property is located within East Boston’s Mixed-Use-7 zoning district and falls within the area covered by PLAN: East Boston, the neighborhood planning initiative adopted by the BPDA Board in January 2024 and incorporated into zoning later that year.

The city’s plan encourages additional housing and mixed-use development around East Boston’s major squares and transit stations while calling for active ground-floor uses.

Planning staff concluded that the Chelsea Street proposal is consistent with those goals. Retail entrances will face Maverick Square, while the residential entrance will be oriented toward the adjoining residential area.

The developer requires zoning relief for lot coverage, side yards and a rear stepback. Planning officials attributed those requests largely to the irregular configuration of the property.

All-Electric, Passive House Design

The building is being designed as an all-electric development using heat pumps for space conditioning and hot water, energy-recovery ventilation, an airtight and highly insulated building envelope and Energy Star-rated appliances.

The project is expected to meet Passive House certification requirements and is designed to be certifiable at the LEED Gold level.

It will also be solar-ready and is registered for the Mass Save Passive House Incentive Program. The developer has committed to purchasing 100 percent renewable electricity for common building loads.

Plans also incorporate stormwater infiltration, green infrastructure, smart streetlights and broadband infrastructure as part of Boston’s Smart Utilities requirements.

Project Advances Following Article 80 Review

The developer filed its Project Notification Form in February. Public review included an Impact Advisory Group meeting on March 10, a public meeting on March 11 and another Impact Advisory Group meeting on May 28.

Community feedback led to changes including increased ground-floor retail, provisions for deliveries and rideshare activity and modifications to the building’s massing and layout.

State Rep. Adrian Madaro submitted a letter supporting the development, citing its housing, affordable housing, transit-oriented location and alignment with PLAN: East Boston.

With the BPDA Board’s approval, the agency’s director is authorized to waive further Article 80 review and issue certifications of compliance once remaining requirements are satisfied. Design review will continue as the developer works toward final construction documents and permitting.

news_communities.summary:
EAST BOSTON, MA — Maverick Landing Community Services (MLCS) officially celebrated the opening of its new Grab & Go Produce Market on July 23, Thursday bringing together more than 70 residents, elected officials, community partners, funders, and volunteers to mark a major milestone in expanding affordable fresh food access and economic opportunity for East Boston families.

The new Grab & Go Produce Market offers a simple, dignified way for residents to access affordable fresh produce and artisan bread while connecting them to a broader network of support services, including housing stability, English classes, workforce development, financial education, and digital literacy.

The celebration featured remarks from Executive Director Rita Lara, State Representative Adrian Madaro, Victor Pelatere from Senator Lydia Edwards’ office, and Gabriella Ramirez from Boston City Councilor Gabriela “Gigi” Coletta Zapata’s office, followed by a citation presentation, a family testimonial, lunch, and guided tours of the new market.

In her remarks, Lara reflected on how the initiative grew from the community’s response during the COVID-19 pandemic. “Six years ago, the pandemic exposed just how fragile food access could be. What began as an emergency response with Fair Foods has grown into a long-term commitment to ensuring every family has access to healthy food with dignity.”

During the pandemic, MLCS partnered with Fair Foods, a 38-year produce rescue organization, to launch four weekly produce markets serving East Boston residents. In 2020 alone, the partnership distributed more than 500,000 pounds of fresh produce throughout the neighborhood.

Since then, MLCS has continued expanding its food access efforts. 

Over the past five years, the organization has distributed more than 1.2 million pounds of healthy food in East Boston. Through its expanded regional food rescue operations, MLCS now expects to rescue and distribute more than 1.2 million pounds of fresh produce and artisan bread annually across Greater Boston.

The Grab & Go Produce Market also represents the next chapter in MLCS’s partnership with Fair Foods. As Fair Foods transitions its leadership after nearly four decades of serving Greater Boston, MLCS is helping preserve and strengthen the organization’s legacy by expanding affordable food distribution throughout the region.

Unlike traditional food distribution models, Grab & Go allows residents to place orders in advance by text or online and pick up their food at a convenient time, reducing wait times and creating a more private, welcoming experience for families. All are welcome! Community residents can sign up for Grab & Go at mlcsboston.org. 

“This model recognizes that people’s lives are busy and that everyone deserves convenient, respectful access to healthy food,” Lara said. “There are no long lines, no unnecessary barriers—just fresh food and a community that cares.”

The new market is also designed as a flexible community space. Throughout the week, it will serve as a classroom for English language learners, host workforce and job readiness activities, provide digital skills support, and offer arts and community programming.

MLCS estimates that families using the Grab & Go Produce Market can save approximately $5,000 to $7,000 annually on grocery expenses, helping reduce financial pressure while improving access to healthy food.

“Today’s celebration is about much more than opening a market,” Lara said. “It reflects our commitment to listening to our community and building practical, innovative solutions that help people thrive. We hope every resident who walks through these doors finds not only fresh food, but also new opportunities and the support they need to build a stronger future.”

About Maverick Landing Community Services

Founded in 2007, Maverick Landing Community Services (MLCS) is a nonprofit community organization serving East Boston residents by building pathways to stability and opportunity. MLCS provides affordable food access, housing stability services, workforce development, adult education, youth programming, financial education, digital literacy, and community health initiatives. With its food expansion MLCS is serving over 5000 residents per year across Greater Boston and is expected to rescue over 1M lbs of produce in 2026.

news_communities.title: Watch: Video shows bicyclist shove man to the ground in East Boston
news_communities.author: Amelia Fabiano and Asher Klein
news_communities.summary:
Surveillance video shows a man who uses a walker being pushed to the ground by someone who’d just ridden past him on a bicycle in East Boston Friday afternoon.

Boston police are investigating the incident, which took place about 3:30 p.m. on Sumner Street near Cottage Street, by a liquor store. They said an elderly man took himself to a local hospital, and had non-life-threatening injuries.

The surveillance video obtained by NBC10 Boston shows a person in a black hooded sweatshirt and backpack riding a bicycle on the sidewalk, knocking over a table set outside before passing the man with a walker.

The cyclist stops, gets off and runs back to the man, then shoves him to the ground.

It wasn’t immediately clear if anyone has been caught. Police were working on sharing more information about what happened.

news_communities.title: Former Mass. teacher charged with rape of child
news_communities.summary:
A former teacher in Lynn, Massachusetts, has been arraigned on a charge of child rape involving a 14-year-old middle school student.

Tymond Tran, 38, of Hudson New Hampshire, appeared in Essex County Superior Court on Wednesday where he pleaded not guilty to rape of a child aggravated by an age difference of ten years or more, indecent assault and battery on a person 14 or over, exhibiting a child in a nude or lascivious pose, and distributing obscene matter to a minor, District Attorney Paul F. Tucker announced.

The alleged crimes occurred during the 2022-2023 school year, when Tran was an eighth-grade teacher at the Thurgood Marshall Middle School in Lynn, the Essex County DA’s office said.

Tran worked in Lynn Public Schools from 2021 to 2024 and left the district on his own, without achieving professional status, according to a statement from Lynn Mayor Jared Nicholson and Superintendent of Schools Molly Cohen that was obtained by the Boston Globe.

“We are shocked and disturbed by this news,” the statement read. “Our primary concern is for the well-being of the former LPS student. Our hope for that student is healing and justice.”

The mayor and superintendent also said they are conducting an independent investigation, and will make support available to the school community.

The Globe additionally reported that Tran was named one of Amazon’s Future Engineer Teachers of the Year in 2024 while he still worked at Thurgood Marshall. He won a $5,000 cash prize for the award, and the school was given $25,000.

Tran most recently worked at Lowell Community Charter Public School, the Globe added. He was “immediately terminated” last month after details of his criminal charges — which do not involve any Lowell Community Charter students — were made available, according to the school’s executive director.

“Like all employees, this individual underwent all required state and federal criminal background checks prior to employment,” Nicholas Leonardos said in a statement to the Globe. “Because the charges were not filed until June 2026, those required background checks did not identify any criminal charges or convictions at the time of hire.”

At Tran’s arraignment on Wednesday, the judge ruled that he must wear a GPS and be on house arrest 24/7 except for emergency medical, court, and attorney visits; have no unsupervised contact with anyone under 18; submit to random device searches; reside at an Attleboro address; stay away from and have no contact with any victim or witness; and not possess any child sexual abuse material.

Tran, who was represented in court by attorney Megan Stanley, is due back for a pre-trial conference on Aug. 26.
