news_communities.title: Teen held without bail on murder charge in Chelsea stabbing
news_communities.author: Mike Pescaro, Marc Fortier, Griffin Gonzalez and Sebastian Agudelo Gomez
news_communities.summary:
A teenager has been charged with murder in connection with a deadly stabbing on Thursday night in Chelsea, Massachusetts.

Sergio Josué Castellanos, 18, was held without bail at his arraignment Friday. He was allowed to hide his face in court.

Police responded to the intersection of Chestnut Street and Everett Avenue around 6:45 p.m. Thursday, and said multiple people were injured in stabbings.

Authorities said Friday that two people were injured: Castellanos, who suffered minor injuries, and 25-year-old Eduardo Rózales López of Chelsea.

Prosecutors with the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office said López was treated at the scene for stab wounds to his neck and torso. He was transported to Massachusetts General Hospital, where he died from his injuries early Friday morning.

Reviewing video, police described seeing five people chasing after López. A man identified as Castellanos could be seen striking López in a stabbing motion while he’s on the ground, prosecutors said.

The video allegedly showed Castellanos and three other people fleeing. Police found him and three other males behind the fence of a home nearby on Chestnut Street.

Castellanos, who was tending to a stab wound to his leg, had changed his clothes from those seen on camera, which were found next to him, prosecutors said. He was transported to an area hospital for treatment.

Authorities said a black machete with stains on the blade was recovered.

Castellanos’ defense attorney, asking that his client be released on bail with GPS monitoring, raised questions about the identity of the attacker. He noted that in the video in which prosecutors described Castellanos making a stabbing motion, no knife was seen.

The judge ordered Castellanos held without bail.

Family members told Telemundo Nueva Inglaterra that López arrived from Guatemala seven years ago and leaves behind a 2-year-old child.

People in the area were shocked by the confrontation.

“It was kind of scary, I’m not going to lie. You still see the remnants of blood on the floor,” neighbor Shauniece White said Thursday. “It’s extremely concerning. As you see, it’s only been one nice day so far. If it’s already happening now, I can only imagine what the summer has in store for us. I’m hopeful that the police will come out and do due diligence to keep the community safe, but wishful thinking in a time like this.”

Massachusetts State Police are assisting Chelsea police with the investigation.

news_communities.title: Danvers murder suspect was spotted wandering around Lynn before his arrest
news_communities.author: Amelia Fabiano
news_communities.summary:
A young man raised alarm on Thursday as he wandered streets and backyards in Lynn, Massachusetts, carrying a knife. Neighbors who saw him were shocked to learn that he’s accused in a murder in Danvers.

Multiple people told NBC10 Boston that they saw 18-year-old Anthony DeMayo walking around at about noon Thursday with a large knife in his hand. Later, he would be identified as the suspect in the murder of Janet Swallow in Danvers.

Several of them called 911, which led police to arrest him in a backyard on Standish Road. The whole thing was caught on home surveillance video.

“They said they saw a crazy guy with a knife, and I’m like, ‘How did this happen,’ you know? It’s scary, you never think, where you live, it’s going to happen,” John Bossi said.

Security cameras captured the moments leading up to the arrest. It starts with a vehicle crashing into Nells Pond in Lynn around 11:40 a.m.

“It’s hard to even get there. I don’t know how he got through. There’s no easy way for a car to get there,” Bossi said.

About 13 minutes later, DeMayo is seen walking down Bow Ridge Road in a bright green shirt, swinging a knife around in his right hand.

Then, he goes to Nells Pond Road. Ashley O’Brien was outside with her ducks when she saw him walk by.

“I thought for sure that this guy was obviously mentally unwell. I didn’t want to make a scene and run away or anything like that, cause he made eye contact with me,” she said.

She immediately called 911, the first of several calls from the neighborhood.

“I just waited till he passed my house, went in, told my husband and called the cops,” O’Brien said. “When we came back out, he was just kind of stabbing all the bushes outside and running a knife across the houses and stuff like that — it was very bizarre.”

Rhonda Deparolesa was another on nearby Standish Road.

“I was sitting on my chair, in the recliner, and all of the sudden, I see somebody jump over my fence,” Deparolesa said. “He just laid flat on his back on the bulkhead and just wasn’t moving, so my husband was upstairs, and I said, ‘Something’s going on here.'”

Deparolesa said he tried to open her door at one point, but thankfully, it was locked.

“What if he did get in my house? My husband and I might not be here,” she said. “You know, you think you’re safe in your house. Sometimes you’re not.”

By around 12:30 p.m., police were after him. They found him in a backyard a few doors down from Deparolesa’s home. He was arrested and placed in a police cruiser.

“I’m just absolutely shocked that a young kid, 18 years old, had his whole life ahead of him, and had to go and do this,” Deparolesa said. “For what? Why?”

Everyone who spoke to NBC10 Boston was shocked to learn DeMayo is accused of murder.

“I just thought this guy needed some help and I just called. I did not think that he’d just murdered somebody,” O’Brien said.

Police confirmed DeMayo was a student at Bishop Fenwick High School in Peabody. They did not comment on the investigation, but said they are fully cooperating with local law enforcement.

Their thoughts and prayers are on the victim, her family, and everyone impacted by the horrific tragedy. They said their focus right now is on staff and students.

They had additional counselors on campus Friday and will on Monday, as well.

news_communities.title: New details revealed in court about Malden teacher accused of raping high school student
news_communities.author: Kaitlin McKinley Becker
news_communities.summary:
A 54-year-old teacher accused of raping a high school student in Malden, Massachusetts, faced a judge Thursday, a day after his arrest.

Authorities allege Scott Marino gave alcohol to an 18-year-old who is known to him and then sexually assaulted her last Wednesday, Feb. 18, at his Stoneham home, where the victim was currently living. Marino was arrested a week after the alleged incident and has been charged with two counts of rape, one count of indecent assault and battery and one count of furnishing alcohol to a person under the age of 21, according to the Middlesex County District Attorney’s Office.

Prosecutors provided shocking new details Thursday in Woburn District Court at the arraignment for Marino, who teaches at Linden STEAM Academy in Malden and coaches the girls’ basketball team at Malden High School.

Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673, and Massachusetts provides this list of statewide and resources for sexual assault survivors.

Jacob McCrindle of the Middlesex County District Attorney’s Office said in court that the alleged victim in this case had been in the foster care of Marino and his wife at the time this occurred. The victim, who moved in with the Marinos at their Stoneham home in the fall, was a basketball player for Marino during the season, and the two were known to each other for many years.

According to prosecutors, Marino’s wife was scheduled to take a trip out of state last Wednesday. The victim was on school vacation, so she went with Marino and a grandfather who lives in a basement apartment at the home to an Ash Wednesday mass. They dropped the older man off at home, and then Marino and the victim went driving because she had a learner’s permit and was learning to drive on the highway. They made the decision to go into Boston to get a takeout seafood dinner, and on the way home, Marino had them stop at a liquor store where surveillance video shows he purchased a strawberry margarita mix, a large bottle of Patron tequila and some other agave liquor.

The two then went back to Marino’s Stoneham home and he allegedly gave her a large margarita. She drank some of it but didn’t like it, though Marino allegedly encouraged her to keep drinking. He later poured them shots of tequila, and they ate the seafood dinner they got. The victim later told police that she was feeling ill so she went to her bedroom where she vomited many times, eventually lying down in bed.

Marino then came in and sexually assaulted her two times, prosecutors said in court. The victim later retrieved her cell phone and began texting friends and ultimately an aunt, begging for help.

McCrindle said that the aunt called 911 as she was driving to the Marino’s home, and the victim was taken to Winchester Hospital for a full sexual assault examination.

“This is a relationship where the defendant was the victim’s foster parent, he took her into his home, that’s a position of trust, as well as coupled with the fact that the defendant is a teacher, or was a teacher at the Malden Public Schools and he was also her coach for many years,” McCrindle said in court, arguing for $100,000 cash bail. “The defendant used I would suggest that relationship, he took advantage of that relationship, there’s a significant age difference, the defendant is 54 years old, the victim is 18 years old. There’s also a significant size difference that’s described in the police report between the defendant and the alleged victim…. it’s also noteworthy that the defendant appears to have waited until his wife left the home so he was more isolated with the victim…clearly some planning went into this.”

Marino’s defense attorney argued before the judge that he’s a respected educator with deep community support who has “never been in court in his life.”

The judge ultimately ordered $75,000 cash bail based on the gravity of circumstances along with several conditions requested by the commonwealth, including that Marino stay away and have no contact from the victim and any witnesses, stay away from all Malden school property and events, be fitted with a GPS bracelet to enforce exclusive zones including the victim’s home address, her school, her workplace and a gym that she frequents, surrender his passport and not be allowed to leave the state.

The judge also added the condition that Marino be alcohol free and submit to SCRAM testing.

Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673, and Massachusetts provides this list of statewide and resources for sexual assault survivors.

Malden Superintendent Timothy Sippel previously said the district was informed Wednesday that Marino had been taken into custody in connection with “a serious incident alleged to have occurred outside of working hours and involving one of our high school students.”

Marino was immediately placed on leave, the superintendent added, noting that the district is cooperating fully with law enforcement agencies in their investigation.

“I understand how upsetting and distressing this is to our community given the serious nature of these allegations,” Sippel said in a statement. “The safety of our students and staff is our highest priority.”

A plea of not guilty was entered on Marino’s behalf. He is due back in court for a probable cause hearing on April 16.

news_communities.title: Girl rescued after falling through the ice in Malden
news_communities.author: Thea DiGiammerino and Mike Pescaro
news_communities.summary:
Firefighters rescued a teen girl who had fallen through the ice into the frigid water of a pond in Malden, Massachusetts, on Wednesday afternoon.

It happened around 2 p.m. at Fellsmere Pond, fire officials said. Firefighters in water rescue suits went in to find the girl holding onto the edge of the ice, according to the Malden Fire Department. She was pulled from the water in under 30 seconds.

“I don’t even think the engine stopped,” Malden Fire Captain Roy Tribble said. “I jumped up, I sprinted down here, pretty much just jumped right into the water.”

The 14-year-old girl was conscious and alert when she was brought to a Boston hospital for treatment.

Tribble said the water was about 30 feet deep.

“A life was saved. It was a young girl who fell through the ice,” added Captain Bob Hegarty.

He warned everyone to stay off thin ice.

“A warning to everybody out there that ice, if it’s not thick enough, you’re going to fall through, and if you fall through, you’re not going to be able to get yourself out,” Hegarty said. “So stay off the ice until it’s very thick, which — who can tell when it’s very thick?”

news_communities.title: Malden woman accused of threatening federal agents making immigration arrest
news_communities.author: Thea DiGiammerino
news_communities.summary:
A Massachusetts woman is accused of threatening to kill federal agents who were conducting immigration enforcement in Malden.

Bethany Abigail Terrill, 37, was charged with threatening a United States official, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said Thursday.

Prosecutors say that Terrill approached the agents as they were making an arrest outside Malden District Court on Sept. 29, describing her as verbally abusive. She allegedly shouted things like “ICE is here, ICE is here,” “You guys are monsters, this is insane,” “Sir, what’s your name, what’s your name,” “I can try to help you,” and “I am an American civilian, I have a right to be here,” and called the agents Nazis.

She is further accused of trying to push past the agents, yelling “Charlie Kirk died, and we love it… We’re coming for you, gonna kill you.” 

According to the statement of probable cause, an agent heard the threat and proceeded to detain Terrill, who they said was “actively resistant and fought to escape.”

Officials say the agents were wearing body cameras, and Terrill was also filming at the time. In the statement of probable cause, investigators say the threat can be heard in the footage from Terrill’s phone.

The agents on scene were from multiple agencies, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), ICE and the FBI.

During her appearance in U.S. District Court in Boston on Thursday, a public defender said Terrill owns a salon and was struggling with legal issues in an unrelated case.

Judge Paul Levenson ordered Terrill be released with conditions, saying “federal agents have a right to not be subjected to threats.”

Terrill was ordered as part of her conditions of release to participate in a mental health program for treatment on a regular basis, to develop a safety plan for her own safety and others, avoid contact with potential witnesses, have no contact with any federal official, family or otherwise in any way or form, refrain from alcohol and the use of any illegal drugs, to avoid contact with law enforcement, and to refrain from making any further threats.

She didn’t speak to reporters outside of court.

The charge of threatening a U.S. official carries a sentence of up to 10 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000.

news_communities.title: Cities bordering Everett unite in Revolution soccer stadium transparency push
news_communities.author: Asher Klein
news_communities.summary:
Four cities that border Everett, Massachusetts, have banded together in a push for more involvement in the New England Revolution’s plans for a soccer-specific stadium in the city.

The mayors of Revere, Medford, Malden and Chelsea formed a coalition called City Mayors for Citizens that they said will seek transparency on plans for the stadium, including the impacts it will have on their communities.

The 25,000-seat stadium proposal has progressed in the state Legislature but still faces plenty of hurdles. The City Mayors for Citizens said they are worried about how the building on along the Mystic River might impact local infrastructure, public transit and quality of life.

“A project of this size and scale will have significant regional impacts,” said Revere Mayor Patrick Keefe Jr said in a statement. “We want to ensure that a stadium is contributing positively to the communities it is drawing resources from. Our residents should not bear the burdens of a private stadium that has strong potential to negatively affect their day-to-day lives.”

Asked for a response to the statement, a Revolution club spokesperson noted that it expects to work with neighboring communities after it reaches agreements with Everett and Boston, which would allow the property to have its port designation removed and the process of construction to continue.

The spokesperson also noted that the team thanked the mayors and promised to review the concerns raised in their letter, sent Monday.

news_communities.title: Video shows Salvadoran man being detained by ICE in Malden
news_communities.author: Oscar Margain, Marc Fortier and Mark Garfinkel
news_communities.summary:
The wife of a Salvadoran man says he was violently taken into custody by immigration officials on his way to work in Malden, Massachusetts, on Wednesday morning.

The incident occurred shortly before 6 a.m. in the area of 28 Kennedy Drive.

Leslie Perlera Gonzalez said she received a distressing call from her husband, Edgar Hernan Elias Escobar, shortly before 6 a.m. as he was heading to his construction job. She rushed to Kennedy Drive, where she said Elias Escobar was surrounded by immigration officers.

“I heard them smash his window, and he was saying, ‘Ow, you’re hurting me,'” Perlera Gonzalez said. “When I arrived on the scene, he had a Taser on his face.”

The 31-year-old had no criminal record and was in the process of adjusting his immigration status after the couple married last year, noted Perlera Gonzalez.

“He’s never come close to doing anything that would be considered a crime,” she said.

She alleged that agents used an unmarked car to ram her husband’s vehicle, forcing him off the road before detaining him.

Malden police said Elias Escobar sustained minor injuries. He was transported on a stretcher to a hospital in Melrose, where Perlera Gonzalez said she was not allowed to see him.

About an hour later, he was moved to a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in Burlington.

A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Elias Escobar was the target of the ICE operation and suffered “no injuries.”

“On September 17, 2025, ICE conducted an immigration enforcement operation in Malden, Massachusetts to arrest Edgar Hernan Elias-Escobar, an illegal alien from El Salvador. During the arrest, the illegal alien refused to comply with officer commands to rolldown his window. The officers took appropriate action and followed their training to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve the situation in a manner that ensured the success of the operation and prioritized the safety of the public and our officers,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “Out of an abundance of caution, ICE law enforcement escorted Elias-Escobar to the hospital for evaluations. Medical staff found he had no injuries and discharged him. He was then escorted to the Boston Filed office for processing and will be placed in removal proceedings.”

“I’ve been expecting this from somebody I know every day since Donald Trump was elected,” said Amiee Parco, an attorney with Greater Boston Legal Services and a colleague of Perlera Gonzalez. “I’ve been waiting for it to affect me personally.”

Friends and coworkers gathered outside the Burlington facility, joining a weekly protest to support Elias Escobar’s release and that of other detainees.

“He’s a really wonderful person,” said Alyssa Rao, a friend of the couple. “I think this is going to impact everyone.”

After Wednesday’s ordeal, Perlera Gonzalez fears what her husband is going through while detained.

“I’m terrified of what could be happening when no one is watching,” she said.

At last check, Escobar was still at the facility. It’s unclear how long he’ll be held — often, people stay several days, though the facility is meant to detain people for hours.

His lawyer is trying to prevent the government from sending him to a far-away detention center, and from deportation.

ICE has ramped up arrests across greater Boston in recent weeks under “Operation Patriot 2.0,” detaining immigrants in public spaces.

Gov. Maura Healey spoke out against the sweeps on Tuesday, saying federal immigration enforcement officers are “creating an incredible amount of fear and intimidation.”

“Some of it seems purposeful, to be honest. Why else are you parked outside a church? Why are you parked outside a community center?”

The governor said her office has received no information from ICE about who is being detained or why.

“This is not a furtherance of public safety,” she said. “In fact, it undermines public safety.”

Asked what she can do to protest White House policy, Healey said: “I join with other governors in urging the Trump administration, in the strongest possible terms, to change course.”

State House News Service contributed to this report.

news_boston.title: Federal Reserve holds rates unchanged, but three members voted to hike amid high prices
news_boston.author: Paul Wiseman | The Associated Press
news_boston.summary:
The Federal Reserve left its key interest rate unchanged Wednesday despite persistently high inflation and a spike in energy prices caused by the Iran war.

The Fed’s rate-setting committee reached the 9-3 decision after two days of deliberations, marking the fifth straight meeting at which the benchmark rate was kept at around 3.6%.

Dissenting in favor of a quarter-point interest rate hike were Beth Hammack, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland; Neel Kashkari, president of the Minneapolis Fed; and Lorie Logan, president of the Dallas Fed.

In reaction to the dissents, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters at a press conference following the Fed’s announcement, “I asked for a good family fight and I got one.”

Inflation has been stuck above the central bank’s 2% target for more than five years. The Iran war has generated uncertainty over the economic outlook and has driven energy prices higher, intensifying inflationary pressure and creating a quandary for Fed policymakers. Hammack, Kashkari and Logan had previously called for or signaled that they would be open to raising rates to combat high prices.

Warsh, presiding over his second meeting of the central bank’s rate-setting committee, has declared that he has “no tolerance” for elevated inflation. He was appointed by President Donald Trump, who has put intense pressure on the Fed to cut rates instead of raising them.

Warsh said in the time between the two latest Fed meetings, the market has reacted to real economic data and the reduction in forward guidance from the central may have played a role in that. The market is “learning to play the ball and not the referee,” Warsh said. The new Fed chair has voiced criticism that his predecessors at the Fed made the markets too dependent on signals from the Fed on the direction of interest rates.

While traders on Wall Street saw a 33% chance the Fed would hike rates Wednesday to tamp down inflation, most expected policymakers to hold off, reluctant to risk disrupting financial markets. But 76% foresee a rate hike in September. A month ago, only 59% of traders expected a September rate increase, according to data from CME.

Fed officials likely want to see more economic data before changing the rate. On Thursday, the Commerce Department delivers the first look at April-June economic growth and it will also publish the Fed’s preferred inflation measure – the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index – for June.

Adding uncertainty to the Fed’s decision-making process is the rising violence in Iran. The price of oil briefly blasted past $100 a barrel last week on intensifying fighting. It’s since settled down on hopes the United States and Iran can find some way to reduce tensions.

Yet early Wednesday, Jordan intercepted missiles launched from Iran early just hours after the U.S. military said it knocked down another Iranian barrage launched against American forces in the Middle East, ending a brief pause in fighting.

After the U.S. and Israel attacks on Feb. 28, Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz – through which a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas pass. That caused the greatest disruption in oil supplies in history and sent energy prices surging. They’ve since bobbed up and down depending on the ever-changing state of the conflict and negotiations to de-escalate it, but the average cost for a barrel is $10 to $15 more today than it was at this point last year.

Inflation has exceeded the Fed’s 2% target since early 2021 when the U.S. economy overheated as it roared back from COVID-19 lockdowns. Inflation peaked at just over 9% in mid-2022 and began to drop in the face of 11 rate hikes by the Fed in 2022 and 2023. But progress has more or less stalled.

Besides the Iran war, other factors adding to inflation pressure are President Donald Trump’s tariffs on foreign goods and a surge of investment in data centers to power artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of computer chips and equipment and electricity.

So-called core inflation – which excludes volatile food and energy prices – cooled in June, partly because apartment rents aren’t rising as fast as they had been. And a temporary drop in gasoline prices last month also helped contain overall inflation.

But several Fed policymakers have been arguing that the Fed will have to raise rates to return inflation to the 2% target.

“Sternly staring at inflation until it melts before our withering gaze is not an option,’’ Christopher Waller, an influential member of the Fed’s governing board, said in a speech this month.

A slow-moving storm has moved overhead and periods of rain over southern New England are expected through Thursday evening.

Rain will be steady at times in the afternoon and evening, with possible bands of heavy downpours. The greatest concern for flash flooding is across western and central Massachusetts, northern Connecticut and northern Rhode Island.

Flash flood warnings were issued Wednesday afternoon for parts of Massachusetts and Connecticut.

A flood watch remains in effect for Worcester County until 8 p.m. Wednesday and for southern New Hampshire until 8 a.m. Thursday.

The flood risk shifts towards Providence and Boston areas during the evening commute.

People may encounter flooded roadways, water-covered underpasses and poor visibility during periods of heavier rain. Small streams and low-lying areas could also see water levels rise quickly.

While the rain gradually becomes lighter on Thursday, cloudy skies and scattered showers linger.

Drier weather is expected to return for much of the weekend before the chance for showers and thunderstorms will increase again early next week.

news_boston.title: Moving on: Four reasons for optimism about what comes next for Celtics
news_boston.author: Chris Forsberg
news_boston.summary:
It’s been a rough couple of months to be a Celtics fan.

Boston fumbled away a 3-1 lead in Round 1 against Philadelphia, spoiling what had otherwise been a highly enjoyable 2025-26 season. The Knicks won a championship and haven’t stopped parading around in the aftermath. The Celtics traded former Finals MVP Jaylen Brown to a division rival, and those Sixers signed LeBron James in the aftermath to create a potential super team. The East as a whole looks as good on paper as it has in decades. 

The duck boats that flowed through downtown Boston just two years ago now feels like two lifetimes ago.

You’ve got two choices, though. You can sit here and wallow in self-pity. Or you can accept that what’s done is done, and move on. We all ran the emotional gamut and navigated the stages of grief that are inevitable when trading a franchise pillar. Some got through it quicker than others. Now it’s time to shift the focus from what happened to what comes next.

This is us channeling our inner Veronica Vaughn. We’re dragging any Billy Madison-looking Celtics fans into the pool and trying to roust you from July’s pity party. I believe in you, Billy (Chisholm). And Brad, too. 

Here are four reasons to be optimistic about what comes next for the Celtics:

MORE CELTICS

Chris Forsberg Jul 22

Is there a case for Bradley Beal in Boston?

Chris Forsberg Jul 23

Brad Stevens locking up Celtics' fleet of young wings

MVP season loading?

Roster construction and money allocation in the apron era played a major role in Boston’s decision to pivot away from Brown, but we thought it was telling that when Celtics president of basketball operations Brad Stevens discussed the trade, he almost immediately pointed to having such a high percentage of usage tied up in two superstars.

Brown finished 36.1 percent of Boston’s possessions during his floor time last season. That wasn’t just a career high, it was the 18th-highest single-season mark in NBA history since usage tracking began in 1978, per Basketball Reference. It was the highest mark in Celtics history and well north of the previous top usage rate set by Isaiah Thomas (33.8 percent) during his magical 2016-17 season.

Maybe Brown would have happily downshifted his usage with a healthier Jayson Tatum on the court this season. Maybe the advanced metrics that showed Boston performed better with Brown off the court in each of the last four seasons would have stabilized. But the Celtics evidently weren’t waiting to find out.

What’s clear now, while the team plots the next iteration of its roster, is that Tatum is going to shoulder the offensive load for the 2026-27 season and probably beyond. If the Celtics were to outkick the downsized expectations amid the departure of Brown, then Tatum is going to thrust himself directly into the same MVP conversation that Brown lingered in last season.

This will be the first time that Tatum has been the sole focal point of the Celtics’ offense. There will be instances where he needs to use that attention to create opportunities for teammates. But Tatum is going to finish a lot of possessions. And his stat line could soar because of it.

Tatum already owns the Celtics’ record for single-season scoring average from the 2022-23 season, when he averaged 30.1 points to go along with 8.8 rebounds and 4.6 assists over 36.9 minutes per game. He finished fourth in MVP voting that year. 

Tatum’s rebounding was off the charts after his return last season (10 rebounds per game in 16 regular-season appearances). He’s averaged a career-best 8.2 assists per 100 possessions in each of his last two seasons. It’s not hard to imagine a particularly glitzy stat line next season. 

In much the same way that Brown thrived as the focal point last year and earned heavy MVP chatter when Boston bested outsider expectations, it feels like Tatum will have the chance to do the same this year. Maybe Victor Wembanyama will simply have a stranglehold on the award moving forward — with Nikola Jokic and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander unlikely to cede their spots at the top of balloting as well. But Tatum will be in the conversation with plenty of possessions available to state his case.

In a big country

Overshadowed by all the Brown drama, the Celtics shored up maybe their biggest area of need last season by signing center Mitchell Robinson. It also created a void for a primary rival by signing away the Knicks’ longest-tenured player and a key piece of their championship bench.

Robinson is a glass-cleaning, country music-loving machine who will turn a whole bunch of Boston’s missed 3-pointers into the second-chance opportunities that Joe Mazzulla so dearly covets. Robinson corralled 21.2 percent of his team’s missed shots last season. That wasn’t just the highest mark in the NBA, it was nearly six percent higher than the next closest player with 1,000+ minutes played (Donovan Clingan, 15.3 percent).

The Celtics know full well how valuable Robinson can be. Mazzulla routinely deployed a Hack-a-Mitch strategy in hopes that New York would take Robinson off the court due to his free-throw woes. Opposing teams will do the same against Boston this year, but Robinson’s impact is undeniable if he stays on the court.

The Knicks’ offensive rebound rate spiked by 9.8 percent per 100 possessions during Mitchell’s floor time last season.  He corralled 31.9 percent of his own misses. His kickouts created some of the most efficient looks that New York got last season.

Can Robinson stay on the floor — both in terms of health and teams targeting his free-throw shooting weakness? That’s a major question for a player who averaged just 19.6 minutes per game over 60 appearances last season, and missed 116 games over the previous two campaigns. 

But his ability to impact winning when he’s on the court is undeniable. He’ll add much-needed depth to a spot that got exposed as Boston fumbled away that 3-1 series lead against the Sixers. His impact could greatly outkick the 9.1 percent of the cap he signed for while inking a 3-year, $47 million deal with Boston.

Kick the player development team into overdrive

Maybe the biggest storyline from last season was the way many of Boston’s youngest players thrived in elevated roles. From Neemias Queta and Payton Pritchard shuffling into starter spots, to recent draftees like Baylor Scheierman, Hugo Gonzalez, and Jordan Walsh all thriving in elevated minutes at various points throughout the 2025-26 campaign, to Luka Garza carving out a role after barely playing at two previous stops, it’s clear the Celtics can maximize their young talent.

Now all those players need to make another leap — or at least find the sort of consistency that the best players in the league bring on a night-to-night basis.

Sure, it would help if Derrick White finds his shot after a rough offensive season. But Pritchard will get every opportunity to be the No. 2 scoring option on the team. Can he eliminate some of the variance in his output, especially when the 3-point shot defies him? His numbers when sharing the floor with Tatum are particularly intriguing.

Can Neemias Queta avoid the sort of foul trouble that forced him off the court too often in the postseason? How many of Boston’s wings will make the sort of leap that makes it easy for Mazzulla to pencil them in for heightened minutes each night?

One thing that could help: The addition of veteran point guard Mike Conley. While Conley’s on-court role might be limited in his age-39 season, he brings 37,588 minutes of regular-season experience. He’s played in 120 playoff games.

To put it another way: Celtics rookie Chris Cenac Jr. was four months old when Conley Jr. was drafted in June 2007. His ability to guide young players could certainly aid Boston’s young nucleus.

The Celtics need to continue to nurture and develop from within.

In Brad We Trust: Optionality and clean books

Look, no one is going to hang a banner for resetting repeater penalties. Or creating optionality. But navigating the second apron and creating windows for increased spending certainly matters in this new apron era. The Celtics are putting themselves in a position to be opportunistic while much of the league is steamrolling towards a reckoning that Boston has already started navigating.

Stevens talked a lot about that optionality in the aftermath of the Brown trade. It’s not fun having to wait for the next shoe to drop, but all the pain points the Celtics have endured the past two summers — from the departures of core championship pieces like Kristaps Porzingis, Al Horford, Jrue Holiday, and Luke Kornet last year; to the shocking Brown trade — have positioned the team to be aggressive with roster construction moving forward.

The next disgruntled NBA star is only a news cycle away. Maybe Denver implodes under the weight of the second apron. Is Anthony Edwards going to stay happy in Minnesota with LaMelo Ball added to the mix? Stars get moved every season, and yet we never stop being surprised when it happens.

The Celtics have the parts to at least get in on the conversation for any players that become available. The team can be judicious in hunting the next star it yearns to pair with Tatum. Maybe the team prioritizes depth and tries to find high-value players on mid-tier salaries to put around Tatum.

Stevens has quietly been locking up depth pieces on team-friendly deals. Queta (four years, $60 million) got a big extension, and Pritchard could soon sign a three-year, $67 million extension. The Celtics inked both Ron Harper Jr. and Jordan Walsh to long-term deals. Neither that duo, nor recent draftees Baylor Scheierman and Hugo Gonzalez will earn more than 3 percent of the cap through their current pacts. 

The Celtics need to maximize their optionality. They need to be willing to spend when free of the repeater shackles next summer. But they’ve created more pathways than previously existed through their often painful maneuvering over the past two summers.

Stevens has thrust himself into a harsh spotlight by trading Brown. There’s going to be pressure to hit a home run on whatever big move comes next. Patience is in short supply in these parts. But Stevens has to show that the Brown trade, painful as it was, was a necessary step in getting the Celtics back to a spot where they can truly compete for a title.

news_boston.title: Two suffer serious burn injuries in separate incidents in Maine
news_boston.author: Sandra Ictech
news_boston.summary:
Two people suffered serious burn injuries in separate incidents in Maine on Tuesday.

A 16-year-old girl was seriously injured after a fire started in the kitchen of her home in Searsport. Investigators said she heard the smoke alarm go off while she was in the upstairs bathroom.

She came downstairs and found the kitchen filled with smoke coming from a pot of cooking oil that was on the stovetop.

As she tried to extinguish the fire, she attempted to move the pot to the kitchen sink. The fire grew larger, causing her to drop the pot. She sustained burns to about 30% of her body, primarily on her legs and torso, and was rushed to Waldo County General Hospital and later transferred to Maine Medical Center in Portland for specialized treatment.

The fire caused only minor damage to the home.

The second incident occurred just before 2 p.m. Tuesday in Parsonsfield.

A 32-year-old man arrived at Sacopee Valley Health Center suffering from burn injuries. Investigators with the State Fire Marshal’s Office later met with the injured man at Maine Medical Center after he was transferred there for further treatment of his burns.

According to investigators, a flash fire started as the man was cutting multiple 50-gallon metal barrels with a cutting torch and one of the barrels with gasoline vapor inside ignited. The man suffered first- and second-degree burns to his abdomen, chest, arms and neck and is expected to make a full recovery.

There was no major damage to the barn area and garage where the fire started.

Both fires have been ruled accidental.

news_boston.title: Should Patriots pursue Vita Vea after Buccaneers star's trade request?
news_boston.author: Nick Goss
news_boston.summary:
The New England Patriots badly need another edge rusher for their defense.

They ranked 26th in total sacks (35) and 20th in sack percentage (5.9 percent) during the 2025 regular season. Edge rusher is a premium position, and New England is one injury away from being incredibly thin in this area.

Rookie Gabe Jacas just recently signed his rookie deal, but he hasn’t been on the field yet at training camp. There are some good veteran pass rushers left on the free agent market, including Jadaveon Clowney.

But there’s also another potential option for the Patriots if they’re looking to bolster their pass rush ahead of the 2026 NFL season.

Vita Vea.

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle requested a trade this week. He’s in the final year of his contract and currently underpaid when compared to other top-tier nose tackles.

Should the Patriots pursue a Vea trade?

The short answer is yes, they should at least explore it.

Even though Vea is a nose tackle and not an edge rusher, he still gets after the quarterback at a high level.

He tallied 4.5 sacks and 16 solo tackles for the Bucs last season. His overall defensive grade of 72.8/100 from Pro Football Focus ranked 20th among interior defensive linemen, and his 77.0/100 pass rush grade ranked 12th-best at the position.

Here’s where Vea ranked in some key stats for his position during 2025, per NextGen Stats:

  • 241 double-teams faced (2nd in NFL)
  • 14 pressures after double team (6th in NFL)
  • 40 total pressures (T-9th among DT)

ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler published a story Wednesday highlighting five potential fits for Vea if he’s traded, and the Patriots were one of them. His list was constructed after a “quick canvas of the league and exchanging a few texts with executives who typically have the pulse on such things.”

Here’s what Fowler said about the Patriots:

“The Patriots are a fit due to their 3-4 defensive front and considerable cap space, as they have nearly $35 million remaining for 2026,” Fowler wrote. “Above all else, New England truly needs an edge rusher. But there aren’t ready-made solutions available at that spot. So, the next best thing would be to locate a disruptor inside to pair with Milton Williams.”

More Patriots coverage

New England Patriots Jul 28

Camp recap: Kayshon Boutte shines, Christian Gonzalez speaks on Day 4

A Williams-Vea duo in the middle of the Patriots’ front seven would be a scary sight for opposing offensive linemen. Add Christian Barmore to the mix and it creates a pretty impressive group.

And even though Vea doesn’t come off the edge, his ability to consistently draw double teams and wreak havoc in the middle of the line would likely make it easier for the edge rushers to get to the opposing quarterback.

What might the Patriots need to give up to make a Vea trade?

“I texted an executive right when this news broke,” ESPN’s Benjamin Solak said Tuesday on SportsCenter, “and I said if you were building a trade package for Vea, what would you do? He said, ‘I don’t know. A second and a fifth?'”

A second- and fifth-round pick is not a small price, especially when you consider the Patriots already parted with a 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick in the A.J. Brown trade.

Vea is 31 years old and entering his ninth pro season. It’s fair to wonder how many more years he has left as a premier player. He’s been pretty durable, though. Vea played all 17 games last season and missed only one game in 2024 and just two in 2023.

If Vea wants a new contract extension, would it make sense to pay him at the top of the market considering his age? Probably not, but it all depends on the details. And if the Patriots did trade for Vea, how would that impact Barmore’s future with the team?

There are plenty of questions to ponder with Vea when assessing a possible fit with the Patriots.

The bottom line is the Patriots need more players who can rush the quarterback, and Vea still does it at a high level. The price might be too high, but the Patriots should at least consider a potential move.

news_boston.title: Teen driver dead in Abington stolen SUV crash, 4 others seriously hurt
news_boston.author: Kaitlin McKinley Becker, Asher Klein and Marc Fortier
news_boston.summary:
A teenager died and four people were seriously hurt when a stolen SUV crashed into a tree in Abington, Massachusetts, as police tried to stop the vehicle Wednesday morning, officials said.

The 17-year-old male driver from Weymouth was pinned inside the SUV with fatal injuries, authorities said. A 14-year-old female passenger was ejected from the vehicle, and the other three passengers who remained inside had life-threatening injuries and were taken to area hospitals and later transferred to Boston hospitals for treatment.

The name of the teen who died has not been released, but Abington Police Chief John Bonney said he spoke with the boy’s mother personally on Wednesday. Police said the others involved the crash ranged in age from 14 to 17.

The crash took place around 8 a.m. on Washington Street near Central Street after an Abington police officer spotted the Hyundai Santa Fe, which had been reported stolen out of Brockton on Tuesday. When the officer tried to pull the vehicle over, the SUV took off at a high rate of speed, apparently left the road and hit a tree.

Video from the scene showed a heavily-damaged red SUV off the side of the road, next to a large tree.

Bonney praised first responders Wednesday for their “heroic efforts” in caring for the crash victims.

Washington Street was temporarily closed between Central Street and Lincoln Boulevard, police said. Motorists were urged to avoid the area and expect traffic delays.

Bonney said the investigation remains active. The officer involved in the chase has been placed on leave for administrative and not punitive reasons, he said. The officer’s name was not released, but Bonney said he has been with the department for under two years.

“This is certainly a traumatic crash,” Bonney said. “This officer, he is just a kind, caring human being, and on a human level, this is difficult.”

news_bc.title: BC To Launch New Krantz Institute for AI, Ethics, and Humanity
news_bc.author: Danica Bergen
news_bc.summary:
Boston College will launch the Krantz Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Humanity to leverage the University’s Jesuit teaching in the study of the technology, it announced earlier this month.

The institute is made possible by a gift from University Trustee Jason Krantz, BC ’95, and Keely Krantz, BC ’95. 

“The gift will establish the Krantz Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Ethics, and Humanity, which will utilize BC faculty, visiting scholars, and industry partners to examine AI’s long-term opportunities and impact from a humanistic perspective, while instilling BC students with the judgement, wisdom, and critical thinking necessary to help them become ethical leaders in its deployment,” the announcement read.

The University did not disclose the size of the couple’s contribution, but called it a “transformative gift.”

Jason is the executive chairman and founder of Definitive Healthcare, a publicly traded data and analytics company. He is also the managing partner and founder of Breachway Capital, a venture firm focused on B2B software, data, and AI innovation. 

“Given Boston College’s commitment to formative education and the Jesuit principles of ethical discernment, BC, in our mind, is uniquely positioned to lead the conversation about the consequences of AI, what the technology means for humanity, and how it might be best leveraged in service to others,” he said in the announcement.

Keely is the president and founder of the O’Dell Women’s Center, a nonprofit organization that provides low-income women in Western Massachusetts with access to career and education opportunities. 

“We want to see values and ethics as foundational components in how the world approaches AI and AI education,” Keely said. “Additionally, we want BC students to use their formative education and discernment skills to help lead and improve the application of AI in the future.” 

BC had already begun investing resources into the study of AI before the Krantzes’ donation. According to the announcement, the University has over 30 faculty members teaching courses concerning AI, and 11 faculty have received external AI-research grants. 

The Krantz Institute hopes to build upon the existing investment by creating internal opportunities and promoting global learning. In addition to offering internships, seed grants, and AI programs to BC students, the institute will also gather pioneering scholars for future conferences and symposia on AI and ethics. 

“Boston College and Boston in general should be the gathering place for discussions where leaders across different fields, including computer scientists, business executives, government leaders, theologians, and ethicists, come together with faculty and students to discuss the impact of this critical technology on the future of humanity,” said Jason. 

Keely added that the institute aims to place the University at the center of human-centered AI innovation. 

“The Krantz Institute aspires to be different from anything we have seen in higher education and will help position Boston College to have a global impact on the future of AI,” said Keely. 

All of BC’s nine schools will be involved in the new institute. 

According to Robert L. and Judith T. Winston Provost and Dean of Faculties David Quigley, BC is aiming to hire an executive director for the Krantz Institute in the 2026–2027 academic year.

In the interim, the institute will be led by Morrissey College of Arts and Sciences Dean Gregory Kalscheur, S.J., and Carroll School of Management John and Linda Powers Family Dean Andrew Boynton.

Kalscheur and Boynton emphasized the potential far-reaching impact of the new institute, which aims to put Catholic, Jesuit thought at the center of AI learning. 

“This investment makes more widely available our faculty’s shared work of inquiry across the disciplines in service of a more just and human future, and enhances our students’ education, helping to form women and men who are not only highly skilled, but also possess sound judgment, careful reflection, and discerning wisdom,” said Kalscheur. 

Boynton noted that the Krantzes’ generosity reflects the University’s fundamental mission. 

“When you combine our enduring motto ‘Ever to Excel’ with the generosity of alumni like Jason and Keely Krantz, Boston College becomes an unstoppable force,” said Boynton.

news_bc.title: 90 St. Thomas More To Become Martignetti Hall After Trustee Gift
news_bc.author: Nikita Osadchiy
news_bc.summary:
Boston College will rename 90 St. Thomas More—a sophomore residential hall located on Lower Campus—Martignetti Hall, following a donation from University alumni Beth V. Martignetti, BC ’76, and Trustee Associate Carmine A. Martignetti, BC ’76, the University announced Tuesday.

“The gift, which comes as the couple celebrates 50 years since their BC graduation, will provide unrestricted support to Boston College, allowing the University and its leadership to address its most urgent needs,” a University announcement said. “In grateful recognition of this gift, Boston College will name the residence hall located at 90 Thomas More Drive Martignetti Hall.”

The University did not disclose the size of the couple’s contribution or specify how it would be earmarked.

In the announcement, the couple thanked outgoing University President Rev. William P. Leahy, S.J., for his contributions, and expressed their enthusiasm for the continuity that his successor, Rev. Jack Butler, S.J., will bring when he steps into the role next month.

“We have so much respect for Fr. Leahy and all that he has done for Boston College, which is now among the best Universities in the country thanks to his leadership,” Beth said in the announcement. “Our appreciation doesn’t end there—we’re so delighted for the transition to Fr. Jack Butler and the continuity that he will bring.”

Leahy is set to resign on July 31 following his historic 30-year tenure.

The now-Martignetti Hall was constructed in 1993, alongside its sister residential dorm, Vanderslice Hall. The building contains 60 residential suites and can house up to 380 students, according to the University website. The hall has maintained its residential address as its title until the donation.

Carmine has been a member of the University’s board of trustees since 2015 and is the president of family-owned Martignetti Companies, a wine, spirits, and beer distributor in New England. He and his wife are residents of Chestnut Hill.

Carmine previously served as the chairman of the Tabor Academy Board of Trustees—a college preparatory boarding and day school in Marion, Mass.—from 2014 to 2021, while Beth worked as a surgical nurse at Brigham and Women’s Hospital following graduation from the University.

The Martignettis did not immediately respond to a request for comment made through their company.

The post 90 St. Thomas More To Become Martignetti Hall After Trustee Gift appeared first on The Heights.

news_bc.title: Reimagining Public Media: NPR’s President Talks Its Current State and Its Future
news_bc.author: Mac Cobb
news_bc.summary:
Over the past year, actions taken by President Donald Trump’s administration have framed public media’s role as a divisive and partisan issue. 

But Katherine Maher sees public media as something that should look to bridge social or political divides.

“No one puts a CNN bumper sticker on their car,” Maher said. “There is a deep, emotional relationship that people have with the idea of being someone who participates in the public media.”

Maher, who has served as the president and CEO of National Public Radio (NPR) since 2024, sat down with The Atlantic’s Evan Smith on May 29 as part of The WBUR Festival in Boston.

Before NPR, Maher was the CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation for five years and served as an adviser to the U.S. Secretary of State’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board from 2022 to 2024. 

Maher began her talk, which was moderated by Smith, by discussing the May 2025 defunding of public media by Trump and Congress, which ultimately cut $1.1 billion worth of funding to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, $120 million of which went to public radio.

“When federal funding was taken off the table by Congress in their decision last year, we knew that there would be a series of consequences,” Maher said.

Those consequences have manifested in recent weeks, as NPR has had to reduce its workforce by 36 people through layoffs, buyouts, or by leaving empty positions unfilled. But Maher is confident that those cuts will end in the near future. 

“You have to do [these cuts] in a way that prevents you from having to go back to that well,” Maher said. “Our goal was to do that. We believe we’ve accomplished that.” 

But with the American public’s trust in media at an all-time low—just 28 percent, according to a recent Gallup poll—Maher sees NPR’s preservation of local media as an important way to keep Americans trusting the news.

“Eighty-five percent of Americans think that local public, not just public media, but local media, is trustworthy and adds value to their community,” Maher said. “The presence of local media is an indicator of lower rates of polarization, greater rates of trust in democratic institutions, but also in your neighbors.” 

With this trust in mind, Maher discussed how people’s decline in radio consumption and changing work habits have forced NPR to adapt its news distribution. 

“We are moving to a model that really encourages digital engagement,” Maher said. “We need to have a digital relationship, because that is where we are today.”

She went on to acknowledge that this movement will force NPR to overcome some of the issues it has had in the past with online coverage.

“There’s a way in the past that the network competed against itself when it came to digital,” she said. “Now my view is that we have to bring everybody together into a singular platform and place where we’re able to say that, you know, all these folks may be consuming information or engaging with everything from Tiny Desk, Morning Edition to your local public affairs show, but they’re doing it in a home that feels like public radio.”

According to Maher, the goal of public media—specifically public radio—is simple: to reduce polarization and get people to recognize each other as people.

“Audio requires you to hear someone—it requires you to listen,” Maher said. “And when we do our work best, we are asking you to listen to someone who you might fundamentally disagree with and also you cannot deny their humanity. That is what public radio can do.”

news_bc.title: BC’s Historic Season Ends With 8–3 Loss to Liberty
news_bc.author: Maria Stefanoudakis
news_bc.summary:
A historic season came to an end on Sunday afternoon as Boston College baseball fell to Liberty for the second time in three days, knocking the Eagles out of the Athens Regional with an 8–3 loss. 

The Eagles, who are coming off the greatest season in program history after winning 17 ACC games and 37 overall, went up 2–0 early in Sunday’s win-or-go-home matchup. But a five-run third inning from Liberty (43–20, 21–9 CUSA) proved too much for BC (37–23, 17–13 ACC) to overcome, and the Eagles exited the game with a trip back to Chestnut Hill looming. 

Ty Mainolfi smacked a home run to right center on just the second at-bat of the game, giving BC an early lead. Brady Miller got off to an efficient start, too, pitching a 1-2-3 first inning. Luke Gallo hit a leadoff double in the bottom of the second, and Gunnar Johnson drove him home with an RBI single. It seemed like the Eagles were rolling. 

Only, that didn’t last. 

Miller retired three batters in order in the bottom of the second, including striking out two. But things started to go south in the third, as a pop up from Jack Toomey stranded Nick Wang on second. The bottom of the frame was when things spiraled out of control. 

A throwing error allowed Liberty to get a runner on second before the Flames had registered a hit. A hit-by-pitch, walk, and a two-RBI single later, Liberty had tied the game. Another BC error—this time in the form of a failed pickoff attempt by Miller—allowed another runner to get home. An RBI triple from Jordan Jaffe and an RBI double from Nick Barone were the icing on the cake. Just like that, Liberty had stolen a 5–2 lead. 

The Flames added on another run in the fourth thanks to a home run from Josh Campos. The Eagles, meanwhile, were unable to generate any offense. Gallo managed a single in the sixth, but that was the Eagles’ only hit after the second inning. 

Liberty scored three more runs across the sixth and seventh innings after Sean Hard relieved Miller. Down 8–2 in the bottom of the seventh, John Kwiatkowski came in for Hard and forced two quick outs to send the game into the eighth. 

Wang and Kyle Wolff both drew walks in the eighth, but a Johnson strikeout ended the frame. Though sophomore transfer John Mitchell was able to silence the Flames in the bottom of the eighth and the Eagles generated one run in the ninth, a Wang flyout ultimately ended BC’s time in Athens—and its season.
